There are thousands of data connectors in your cloud service provider. Have any of them changed since the last time you reviewed them? Good luck hunting for a specific needle in a stack of needles.
tools: Check with your cloud provider and see what tools they provide. It's ok, you're paying them a ton of money for all this.

data.name: Permissions Audit
data.description: Users can have everything by default... which makes your organization vulnerable by design. Who gets to do what and why? Who is the magical unicorn that gets the exceptions? Are permissions open for convenience? When was the last time you fixed something a security audit didn't make you do? You can be the decider if you want--the power is yours!

data.name: Microsoft Direct Phishing
data.description: The attackers found your public Microsoft 365 smart host mail endpoint and delivered a phishing email to an end user, bypassing your spam filtering. They harvested the end user's credentials.

data.name: Wi-Fi Guest Network Escape
data.description: The attackers abused your open guest network. A misconfiguration allowed them access to the production network.

data.name: Publicly Exposed Secret Key
data.description: The attackers compromised your network after a developer pushed an application secret access key to a public Git repository.

data.name: Vendor Default Credentials Attack
data.description: The attackers examined public vendor documentation, finding the default passwords to one of your remote services, granting them access.

data.name: Vishing
data.description: The attackers spoofed the help desk caller ID, convincing an employee to provide credentials in order to complete an "urgent task."

data.name: Trojan Mail
data.description: The attackers shipped enticingly labeled USB devices with autorun malware to remote employees' homes. Multiple employees connected them to their workstations, allowing the malware to beacon back to the attacker.
tools: A USB device loaded with malware (ex. PlugX) and a little luck.

data.name: HTML Smuggling
data.description: The attackers obtained a remote shell on an endpoint by convincing a user to execute malware utilizing a well-disguised .html attachment.

data.name: Insecure Internet of Things (IoT)
data.description: The attackers exploit IoT devices accessible from the production network, allowing them to pivot to other network segments.

data.name: Misconfigured Certificate Template
data.description: The attackers request a vulnerable certificate template from your Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) server.

data.name: NTLM Abuse
data.description: The attackers perform a New Technology LAN Manager Version 1 (NTLMv1) downgrade attack by coercing authentication from a target host.

data.name: Dumping LSASS Via Task Manager
data.description: The attackers utilize local admin access to perform a memory dump of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) process using Task Manager.

data.name: Default Administrator Credentials
data.description: The attackers were able to identify a device that was still configured with the default credentials. A single web search was all it took to gain admin access to your machines.

data.name: Decrypting LSA Secrets
data.description: The attackers utilize local admin access to query the registry and find credentials stored within the Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets.

data.name: SUID Permissions Abuse
data.description: The attackers identify and exploit a binary with Set User ID (SUID) permissions.

data.name: MachineAccountQuota (MAQ) Abuse
data.description: The attackers identify and abuse the MachineAccountQuota (MAQ) attribute to create a new machine account in the domain.

data.name: Group Policy Object (GPO) Modification
data.description: The attackers modify a Group Policy Object (GPO) to create a scheduled task which reestablishes a beacon.

data.name: Golden Ticket Attack
data.description: The attackers steal the Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket (KRBTGT) account credentials and issue TGTs outside the network.

data.name: Screensaver Hijack
data.description: The attackers modify the screensaver path to create a reverse shell triggered by user inactivity. Unfortunately, this exciting new virtual fishtank screensaver has end users hooked, and they might fight efforts to remove it.

data.name: SSH Authorized Keys Modification
data.description: The attackers add their own SSH public key to a user's authorized_keys file.

data.name: Unauthorized Filesharing Utility
data.description: The attackers take advantage of an employee's unsanctioned "shadow IT" cloud-based filesharing resource to exfiltrate data.

data.name: Misuse of Remote Access Software
data.description: The attackers install a trusted and commonly used remote access software in the environment.

data.name: Hosted Note Taking as C2
data.description: The attackers use a trusted note-taking application to publish commands, allowing malware to fetch and execute.

data.name: Bluetooth as Exfil
data.description: The attackers enable Bluetooth and then lurk within the broadcast range (33') to exfiltrate data.

data.name: Crank Up the Pressure
data.description: The attackers have started contacting your clients stating that they have compromised personally identifiable information (PII) and your company was not willing to protect it. Word spreads quickly on social media.
data.notes: Leadership is demanding results faster than you can possibly deliver, the Defenders lose 1 turn.

data.name: Communication Infrastucture DDoS
data.description: An attack group unrelated to the current scenario runs a DDoS attack against your communications infrastructure during the incident.
data.notes: The Defenders must use an alternative form of communication for the next two turns.

data.name: Way to Plan Ahead
data.description: The security team brought on DenSecure™ for threat emulation against known threat actor behavior. The team has implemented new detections that caught the attacker's persistence actions within the network.
data.notes: The Incident Captain must reveal the Persistence card.

data.name: Water, Water Everywhere!
data.description: A pipe bursts in the server room. Seems like a good time to model that new flower print bathing suit while the backup site is brought online.
data.notes: The Defenders receive a -3 modifier for the next two turns.

data.name: Timber!
data.description: A tree falls and knocks out power to your office -- time to head to a secondary location. Unfortunately, traffic is terrible and you'll be stuck in the car for a while.
data.notes: The Defender who rolled the die and caused this Inject can't help the team for three turns while they're stuck in traffic.

data.name: It's a Feature, not a Bug
data.description: A penetration test reveals a critical severity issue in one of your core technologies that the vendor claims is a feature, not a bug. The Defenders implement their own defenses to mitigate exploitation.
data.notes: The Defenders receive a +2 modifier on all Procedure cards for the rest of the session.

data.name: Dude...Where's My Server?
data.description: Your organization's users contact the helpdesk saying all of their fileshares are missing. Security footage reveals an unknown person absconding with the physical drives.
data.notes: Server Analysis is unavailable to the Defenders for the rest of the session -- in addition, they lose 1 turn as they figure out whose problem this is.

data.name: Executive Buy-In
data.description: An at-home PC compromise has your CEO's personally identifiable information (PII) all over the web. Suddenly, management cares a lot about security and has approved all of the team's training requests.
data.notes: The Defenders receive a +2 modifier on all Procedure cards for the rest of the session.

data.name: Call a Consultant
data.description: Do you want help? Feeling stuck? Rolling badly? Need a different perspective on the incident? Then maybe it's time to phone a friend. You can choose one Consultant Card to help your team with the incident. The Consultant Card's modifier is effective immediately.

data.name: Exchange Zero-Day Vunlerability Exploit
data.description: The attackers exploited a previously undisclosed vulnerability (known as a zero-day) on an unpatched Exchange server to gain remote access into the network.

data.name: Fake Software Updates
data.description: A user installed a fake software update, which instructed them to call a "support" number. The attackers established a remote support session in order to exfiltrate data.

data.name: Embedded Remote Access Trojan (RAT)
data.description: The attackers gained access to the network by exploiting multiple endpoints that were using pirated software that contained a Remote Access Trojan (RAT).

data.name: Public Facing Database Compromise
data.description: The attackers discovered a database exposed to the public internet. Using known SQL injection techniques, the attackers executed a malicious script on the server, giving them access to the internal network.

data.name: Malware Propagation
data.description: The attackers leverage a worm (a type of trojan designed to replicate and spread) that slithers through the network.

data.name: Unpatched Critical Security Update
data.description: The organization ignored a critical security patch because of the time and labor cost. The attackers exploit the vulnerability and elevate their privileges to administrator level.

data.name: Living Off The Land
data.description: The attackers use a trusted Remote Monitoring & Management (RMM) application to maintain access.

data.name: Hiding in Plain Sight
data.description: The attackers set exclusions in the antivirus software allowing them to operate undetected with innocently-named scheduled tasks.

data.name: Registry Modification
data.description: The attackers set a script to run via a registry key. This creates a backdoor for future access using a built-in application and native scripting language. This will execute automatically as the user logs in.

data.name: WMI Events
data.description: The attackers set a Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) event subscription that establishes remote system access five minutes after restarting the endpoint.

data.name: Clipboard Scrape
data.description: The attackers scrape clipboard content and exfiltrate data.

data.name: Rotating C2 Server Location
data.description: The attackers place an encoded URL within the comment section of a celebrity's social media account allowing them to obfuscate the location of their C2 server.

data.name: Security Awareness Training for the Win!
data.description: The Defenders had Security Awareness Training set up for the employees. This raised the general security posture of the organization. Good job!
data.notes: The Defenders receive a +3 modifier for the next three turns.

data.name: Ignore Those Pesky Open Ports
data.description: A server has Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) exposed on the internet and nobody checked Huntress External Recon to identify this threat. A new attacker has come in during the middle of the incident.
data.notes: The Incident Captain draws an additional Initial Compromise card.

data.name: A Bad Day Made Worse
data.description: The Threat Research team at Huntress discloses a zero-day vulnerability in the Defenders' business-critical software package and it must be addressed immediately.
data.notes: The Defenders lose 1 turn.

data.name: Haste Makes Waste
data.description: The Defenders didn't consult their cyber insurance provider before starting the incident response (IR) plan. Remediation efforts are delayed while the preferred IR vendor is brought up to speed.
data.notes: The Defenders lose 1 turn and must explain how they will proceed.

data.name: Alert Fatigue is Real
data.description: The Defenders' endpoint detection and response (EDR) solution was not managed.
data.notes: The Defenders receive a -3 modifier on Endpoint Security Protection Analysis for the rest of the session.

data.name: Knowledge is Power
data.description: The Defenders attended a recent Huntress Tradecraft Tuesday episode about "Quick Forensics for the Lazy Investigator." This taught the Defenders the latest persistence techniques used by attackers.
data.notes: The Incident Captain must reveal the Persistence card.

data.name: That Was a Bad Idea
data.description: The host isolation feature in the Huntress platform was disabled by the Defenders, allowing the attackers to move freely through the environment.
data.notes: The Incident Captain draws an additional Pivot and Escalate card.

data.name: Read to The End
data.description: The Defenders neglected to perform a root cause analysis (RCA) and the attackers easily regain control.
data.notes: The Incident Captain draws an additional Persistence card.

data.name: Back to Basics
data.description: The Defenders configured their monitoring tools to alert when security tools stop working. The attackers disabled the endpoint detection and response (EDR) solution and the Defenders were alerted immediately.
data.notes: The Defenders receive a +3 modifier on Endpoint Security Protection Analysis for the next time it's used.

data.name: Rookie Mistake
data.description: An entry-level tech neglected to read an incident report that instructed them to block a known C2 server IP address at the firewall. Dammit, Bobby!
data.notes: The Incident Captain draws an additional C2 and Exfil card.

data.name: A Little Help From My Friends
data.description: The Defenders have been investing time and resources into cybersecurity peer groups, developing relationships with fellow professionals to help each other in times of need.
data.notes: The Defenders draw a Consultant card of their choosing.

data.name: Risk Accepted
data.description: Turns out the endpoint detection and response (EDR) solution was only installed on "business critical" servers. Management wouldn't approve the cost of covering all devices.
data.notes: Endpoint Security Protection Analysis is unavailable for the rest of the session.

data.name: Major Failure Alert
data.description: The Defenders disabled multi-factor authentication (MFA) for a third-party vendor's service account to access the internal network. This allows attackers to spread further throughout the organization.
data.notes: The Incident Captain draws an additional Pivot and Escalate card AND Persistence card.

data.name: Let's Rock
data.description: The Defenders' Lead Incident Responder decides to reinvent themselves as a rock musician and goes on tour.
data.notes: All procedures receive a -1 modifier for the rest of the session.

data.name: Kyle Hanslovan
data.description: (+3) Modifier for dice rolls for the next (3) turns
data.quote: "Every person you admire in cybersecurity also struggles with imposter syndrome." — Kyle Hanslovan

data.name: John Hammond
data.description: The Incident Captain must reveal the Pivot and Escalate Card
data.quote: "Show, not tell; facts, not fear." — John Hammond

data.name: Matthew Brennan
data.description: The Incident Captain must reveal the C2 and Exfil Card
data.quote: "Decode all the things." — Matthew Brennan

data.name: Jamie Levy
data.description: The Incident Captain must reveal the Persistence Card
specialties: Lover of Farming, Fishing, and Music
data.quote: "The more you know, the more you realize there’s so much more you don’t know." — Jamie Levy

data.name: Harlan Carvey
data.description: For the next (2) turns, each of the Defenders roll a D20 and use the highest number
data.quote: "Keep calm and DFIR on." — Harlan Carvey

data.name: Cat Contillo
data.description: The Defenders receive an extra (3) turns to complete the session
specialties: Champion of Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging
data.quote: "When the infosec industry supports culture add vs culture fit, diversity will continue to strengthen and help cultivate innovative brilliance." — Cat Contillo

data.name: Vendor Portal
data.description: A vendor portal had been added to the network that created a path into your organization, bypassing all security controls. The attackers scanned this system and deployed malware to it.

data.name: Dual-Homed Device
data.description: An operator connected an engineering workstation (EWS) directly to the internet via a secondary network interface. The attackers found that host on Shodan, and they brute force attacked it to gain access.

data.name: Infected Authorized Vendor Laptop
data.description: An ICS vendor arrived on-site to perform maintenance and plugged in an infected laptop. The malware propagated to local systems. This gave the attackers access to the network even after the vendor left the site.

data.name: Data Historian Compromise
data.description: The attackers have compromised the IT network and discovered that a data historian in the ICS network is exposed due to permissive firewall rules. The attackers gained access to the ICS network through this historian.

data.name: IT Compromised With Shared Domain Trust
data.description: The attackers have compromised the enterprise domain controllers (DC). They moved laterally to devices in the ICS network that shared trust with the DC.

data.name: Dirty USB
data.description: With a boring night shift, the plant operator brought in downloaded movies on a USB drive that contained malware. Upon insertion, the malware automatically infected the system and beaconed home.

data.name: Exploitable API
data.description: A device is deployed to the ICS network with an internet-exposed API for a predictive maintenance system. The attackers took advantage of an available exploit of the API to gain access and control of the underlying device.

data.name: Insider Threat
data.description: A disgruntled internal user purposely allowed attackers to gain access to devices in the ICS network that they control.

data.name: Malicious Project Files
data.description: The attackers take control of an engineering workstation (EWS), modify the project files, and push them to controllers.

data.name: EWS Issues Rogue Command
data.description: The attackers leverage an engineering workstation (EWS) to issue industrial commands directly to controllers.

data.name: Modifying Read/Write Scripts
data.description: The attackers locate and modify scripts used for ICS network and system administration with write permissions. These scripts are linked to scheduled tasks.
tools: Your Politically-Charged Text Editor of Choice

data.name: Internal Password Spray
data.description: The attackers use default passwords to spray and access systems in the ICS network.

data.name: Broadcast/Multicast Protocol Poisoning
data.description: For years, LANMAN was the worst thing in Windows. Then LLMNR said, "Stand Back and Hold My Beer!" Basically, LLMNR lets a host ask for name resolution from any system on the same network. The attackers perform Broadcast/Multicast protocol poisoning on your Active Directory Network.
tools: Responder Attacks LLMNR, NBT-NS, WPAD, and mDNS.

data.name: New Service Creation/Modification
data.description: The attackers create and load their malware using a new service or existing service modification.

data.name: Local Privilege Escalation
data.description: The attackers use a misconfiguration or vulnerability in local software to gain administrative access.

data.name: GPO Push of Scheduled Tasks
data.description: The attackers leverage access to the domain controller (DC) for the industrial environment. They push scheduled tasks to all hosts enrolled in the domain in order to access and control every device.

data.name: Stolen Engineering Workstation (EWS) Account
data.description: Logon credentials for all engineering workstations (EWS) in the industrial environment are shared and weak. The attackers crack and repeatedly use them to access multiple Windows workstations.

data.name: Malicious Logon Scripts
data.description: A local logon script runs at each user logon to build their session and auto-launch the human-machine interface (HMI) application. The attackers discover that the logon script is editable by any user on the host and modify it.
tools: Your Politically-Charged Text Editor of Choice

data.name: GPO Modification
data.description: The attackers discover an account with permissions to modify a GPO that is linked to all Windows systems on the domain. They modify it to schedule a custom Windows service that launches a payload and establishes callbacks to C2 infrastructure.

data.name: Malicious Report Macros
data.description: Automated daily production reports were built using an outdated spreadsheet that retrieves summarized production data from the distributed control system (DCS). The attackers introduce a malicious macro to call back to a local C2 proxy.
tools: Excel '97 and... a Dream of Evil

data.name: HMI Graphics Manipulation
data.description: The attackers modify an OnLoad.vbs script that a local human-machine interface (HMI) relies on.
tools: Your Politically-Charged Text Editor of Choice

data.name: Malicious Firmware
data.description: The attackers leverage access to an engineering workstation (EWS) to deploy trojanized firmware to devices.

data.name: Autorun Malware
data.description: The attackers modify a system so that malicious code is launched by the operating system during startup.

data.name: New User Added
data.description: Easy, the attackers add a new user to the local computer.

data.name: Accessibility Features
data.description: The attackers hijack Accessibility Features like Sticky Keys and On-Screen Keyboard.

data.name: Screenshot Exfil
data.description: The attackers leverage access to the network to conduct reconnaissance of human-machine interfaces (HMI) by taking screenshots and exfiltrating them in unencrypted .jpg format.

data.name: Bridged System
data.description: A bridged system was installed in the DMZ that has open file-shares for both the IT and ICS networks. The attackers use this share to move data across the IT/ICS DMZ without passing through the firewall or monitoring.

data.name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium
data.description: The attackers use a USB drive, printouts, or even socks... yes, socks, as a way to get data out of a network. This requires an accomplice on the inside or it can be used with the Insider Threat (Initial Compromise) card.
tools: USB Drive/Socks and a Dream... a Dream of Evil.

data.name: HTTP as Exfil
data.description: The attackers use HTTP as an exfil method. This is usually used in conjunction with some type of stego. For example, VSAgent uses Base64 encoded __VIEWSTATE as an exfil field.

data.name: TCP Handshake as Morse Code
data.description: The security controls allow outbound TCP SYN packets through before killing a session, so the attackers are using SYN packets as a form of Morse code to get signal out.
tools: Anything That Can Start a TCP Session

data.name: DNS as C2
data.description: The attackers use DNS as a C2 channel.

data.name: Sequence of Events (SOE) Analysis
data.description: Reviewing the data historian and Sequence of Events (SOE) recordings can determine which part of the process showed signs of impact, during what time period this occurred, and in what order.

data.name: Protocol Analysis
data.description: Examining the traffic on a network can determine what systems should be talking and what systems shouldn't be talking to each other on specific protocols.

data.name: Cyber Deception
data.description: The attackers go after one of your deception technologies. This could be a word web bug, honey account, or a full honeypot.

data.name: Site Walkthrough
data.description: Sending personnel to the site to examine the written logs, look for wireless access points, physical ingress methods, and equipment stacks can help identify abnormalities.

data.name: Shodan Review
data.description: ICS equipment shouldn't be visible directly from the internet, but stuff happens. By looking for hostnames, certificates, keywords, and other fingerprints, you can find "air-gapped" systems enumerated in Shodan.

data.name: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis
data.description: Yeah... good luck with this one. Are you logging the right things? Do you regularly emulate attack scenarios to see if you can detect them?

data.name: Firewall Log Review
data.description: Can your organization analyze and understand firewall logs? Do you regularly emulate attack scenarios and verify that your procedures work?

data.name: Consequence-Driven Threat Hunting
data.description: Does your team consider their worst industrial consequences, track down what systems could cause those hazards, what mitigations are in place, and use those to map attacker tools, tactics, and procedures to hypothesize and hunt for malicious activity?

data.name: Employee Interviews
data.description: Your team gets to interview the operators, architects, vendors, security personnel, and management at the site of the incident.

data.name: User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA)
data.description: It's like logging, but it actually works. User and entity behavior analytics (UEBA) looks for multiple concurrent logons, impossible logons based on geography, unusual file access, password sprays, and more!

data.name: Endpoint Analysis
data.description: This is where the Defenders use their SANS IR Cheat Sheets to detect attacks on workstations. Time to bring in a local operator... and hope for the best.

data.name: Memory Analysis
data.description: The Defenders pull the memory from the suspect system and review it for possible malicious activity.

data.name: Unexpected PLC State Change
data.description: A programmable logic controller (PLC) has exhibited an unexpected start/stop state change. This indicates the attackers are currently active.
data.notes: The Defenders receive a +2 modifier for Protocol Analysis on their next turn for knowing where to look.

data.name: Safety Instrumented System (SIS) Tampering
data.description: A safety instrumented system (SIS) goes offline, and when the maintenance crew examines it, the firmware checksum does not match.
data.notes: The Defenders receive a +2 modifier for Endpoint Analysis on their next turn for knowing where to look.

data.name: Mediation
data.description: The Defenders have to function as mediators between the IT and ICS network teams.
data.notes: All future turns receive a -1 modifier until they reveal an Attack Card, then all turns thereafter receive a +1 modifier for the goodwill period.

data.name: You Can't Get There From Here
data.description: Due to the remote location and travel logistics, the Defenders have to walk a site operator through the evidence collection process.
data.notes: They receive a -1 modifier on Endpoint Analysis and Memory Analysis for the rest of the session.

data.name: Emergency Facility Shutdown
data.description: A compromise of a hazardous material container causes an immediate evacuation of the production facility. This is where all of the backbone ICS routers are located.
data.notes: The Defenders lose 1 turn.

data.name: Legacy Knowledge
data.description: The Defenders must roll again to see if the person who built the system is still working at the site.
data.notes: (1-10) means the happily retired individual is not there to assist them. -2 modifier on the next turn (11-20) means the grizzled veteran that deployed the legacy system still works at the site to assist them. +2 modifier on the next turn

data.name: No High Availability (HA) System
data.description: Current endpoint investigations are on fragile systems that are without redundancy.
data.notes: The Defenders are limited to collecting information with the tools already installed. They receive a -2 modifier on Endpoint Analysis and Memory Analysis for the next two turns.

data.name: No Shirt, No Shoes...
data.description: Half of the Defenders have been deemed to be wearing inadequate personal protective equipment (PPE). They may not enter the site until they acquire full leather uppers and cotton clothes.
data.notes: The Defenders may elect to receive a -4 modifier on their next turn OR lose 1 turn and receive a +4 modifier on the turn thereafter.

data.name: USB Worm
data.description: The USB devices used for collecting information become infected with autorun malware.
data.notes: The Defenders receive a -2 modifier on Endpoint Analysis and Memory Analysis for the next two turns.

data.name: Call a Consultant
data.description: Do you want help? Feeling stuck? Rolling badly? Need a different perspective on the incident? Then maybe it's time to phone a friend. You can choose one Consultant Card to help your team with the incident. The Consultant Card's modifier is effective immediately.

data.name: Physical Security Review
data.description: Do you have security cameras? Do you have security guards? Do you have access badges for certain areas in your facilities? Can just anyone access your sensitive IT infrastructure? No? Are you sure?

data.name: USB Drive-By
data.description: An employee picked up a worm on their work machine after plugging their USB device into a communal computer at a print shop, giving the attackers access to the internal network.

data.name: Compiled After Delivery
data.description: The attackers assembled their files on an endpoint by delivering text-based source code and using that compromised system's native compiler.

data.name: Gatekeeper Bypass
data.description: The attackers bypassed Apple's Gatekeeper functionality and tricked a user into downloading a malicious file on a macOS endpoint.

data.name: Obfuscated Payload Delivery
data.description: The attackers installed a malicious executable that evaded signature-based analysis by encoding and splitting its payload.

data.name: RFID Thief
data.description: The attackers used a Flipper Zero to copy the Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) signal from an IT employee's entry badge and gained physical access to the server room.

data.name: Disabling Windows Defender
data.description: The attackers use PowerShell commands and scripts to disable Windows Defender, enabling them to bypass file inspection controls designed to prevent malware.

data.name: Process Injection
data.description: The attackers inject their payload into a legitimate, privileged process.

data.name: LSASS Credential Dump
data.description: The attackers dump the contents of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) process memory, gaining access to legitimate account credentials.

data.name: Application Control Bypass
data.description: The attackers use Rundll32 to execute malicious code while avoiding detection.

data.name: Read/Write With chmod 777
data.description: The attackers turn their attention to your*nix machines and want all the permissions! They're using misconfigured user and group permissions to run in a different user's context.

data.name: PsExec Abuse
data.description: The attackers use PsExec to move laterally and gain control of additional systems.

data.name: Lateral Tool Transfer
data.description: The attackers move a malicious payload from a system they initially compromised to a new host on the same network.

data.name: Authorized Remote Tools
data.description: The attackers use an authorized remote administration tool to exfiltrate confidential information.

data.name: Cloud Services as Exfil
data.description: The attackers hitch a ride on the application access tokens for your cloud-based resources. It's a good thing they didn't crash your Kubernetes, but not all is well; they leverage your API to exfiltrate data.

data.name: Bluetooth as Exfil
data.description: The attackers knew you were watching that wired connection closely and got crafty—they exfiltrate all that valuable data via a Bluetooth-enabled device.

data.name: Malicious Access Point
data.description: The attackers hide an access point spoofing a legitimate ESSID in a plant pot in the lobby! Unsuspecting employee devices connect to it when they're nearby. This is a Machine-in-the-Middle (MitM) strategy.

data.name: Event-Triggered Execution
data.description: The attackers use a permanent WMI event subscription to execute a malicious payload anytime the user logs in.

data.name: Scheduled Task
data.description: The attackers have made themselves immortal by using a scheduled task on a Windows system to persistently run malicious code every 30 minutes.

data.name: Rename Process
data.description: The attackers change the name of a system utility to make their malicious executions look benign.

data.name: Spawn Web Shell
data.description: The attackers abuse the Internet Information Services (IIS) worker process to install a web shell on a Windows web server.

data.name: Missed Payday
data.description: The attackers compromise your email account, email HR, and instruct them to update your direct deposit information, routing your paycheck into a bank account they control.
data.notes: Each of the Defenders must roll a D20 and the person with the lowest number has to get a night job as a bartender and must remain silent for the rest of the session.

data.name: Not a Red Team
data.description: The network threat-hunting team has detected C2 beacons on multiple machines in your environment. The attackers can now install additional payloads on the affected machines.
data.notes: Have the Incident Captain draw an additional Persistence Card as well as a Pivot and Escalate Card.

data.name: Deez Registry Keyz Plz?
data.description: A wild malicious registry key appears. The bad news: It is on 50 endpoints that are now rampant with malware. The good news: Management cares.
data.notes: The Defenders get 3 additional turns to help solve the incident and a Consultant Card of their choice without rolling a D20.

data.name: Nuclear Test Site
data.description: Thank goodness the Defenders are Atomic Red Team™ power users and they are prepared for all the endpoint threats.
data.notes: The Defenders receive a +2 modifier on Endpoint Analysis and Endpoint Security Protection Analysis for the rest of the session.

data.name: Quishing
data.description: The local burger joint uses a QR code for its menu. How convenient! Unfortunately, a disgruntled ex-analyst knows the Defenders are regulars and put a malicious QR code over the legitimate one. Anyone who scanned it compromised their MFA device, which now needs to be wiped or replaced.
data.notes: The Endpoint Security Protection Analysis card is unavailable for the next two turns.

data.name: Cat on Keyboard Deletes Production Database
data.description: Curiosity killed the database entries! A work-from-home administrator left their computer unlocked and, in an attempt to gain additional snuggles, their cat happened to spam out a mass delete on their keyboard. Oops.
data.notes: Each of the Defenders must roll a D20. The first two people to roll an odd number have to go fix the database and must remain silent for the rest of the session. Even number rollers move on to finish the incident.

data.name: Undocumented System
data.description: That asset management and discovery project probably shouldn't have been put on hold. An undocumented system was just found on the enterprise domain and we don't really know anything about it. Who knows when this thing was spun up and for what?
data.notes: The machine had 200 Bitcoin from 2010. The Defenders order pizza and discuss if they're going to tell management or not.

data.name: Sneaky Sneaky RAT
data.description: The attackers gain a foothold in the environment via remote access trojan (RAT). Now they're using it to load in external files and tools to further their reach. If this isn't under control soon, you'll have more than just RATs to worry about.
data.notes: Have the Incident Captain pull another set of Attack Cards. The Defenders get five extra turns.

data.name: Adam Mashinchi
data.description: The Incident Captain must reveal the C2 and Exfil Card
data.quote: "Keep in mind that for the adversary, tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) are side effects, not the intent." — Adam Mashinchi

data.name: Carrie Roberts
data.description: The Incident Captain must reveal all cards that list Atomic Red Team™ as a tool
data.quote: "Prevention is ideal, but detection is a must." — Anonymous

data.name: Mike Haag
data.description: The Incident Captain must reveal all cards that list SIEM as a detection source
data.quote: "I am everywhere and nowhere." — The Haag

data.name: Cloud Event Log Analysis
data.description: Are you missing what should be in your cloud logs? Do you even know what cloud provider logs you need in an incident response situation? There are thousands of data connectors in your cloud service provider. Have any of them changed since the last time you reviewed them? Good luck hunting for a specific needle in a stack of needles.
tools: Check with your cloud provider and see what tools they provide. It's ok, you're paying them a ton of money for all this.

data.name: Permissions Audit
data.description: Users can have everything by default... which makes your organization vulnerable by design. Who gets to do what and why? Who is the magical unicorn that gets the exceptions? Are permissions open for convenience? When was the last time you fixed something a security audit didn't make you do? You can be the decider if you want--the power is yours!

data.name: Call a Consultant
data.description: Do you want help? Feeling stuck? Rolling badly? Need a different perspective on the incident? Then maybe it's time to phone a friend. You can choose one Consultant Card to help your team with the incident. The Consultant Card's modifier is effective immediately.

data.name: Forest Trusts
data.description: Despite your protests, your parent company insisted on maintaining an admin account in your forest (which resides in their forest). The attackers compromised your parent company's forest and pivoted into your forest. Thanks, parent company.

data.name: AI Generated Script
data.description: ChatGPT (and other LLMs) "cannot provide scripts or advice for illegal activities," but the attackers are smarter than the bot. They used a unique AI-generated script to bypass security controls and gain access to the environment.

data.name: SSO Provider Compromise
data.description: The attackers -- some cheeky teenagers -- vished their way into your single sign-on (SSO) provider's system and pivoted into your internal network, email, and SaaS applications.

data.name: Weaponized Hardware Security
data.description: The attackers visited your corporate headquarters and found a domain-joined computer sitting in the lobby in "locked down" kiosk mode. What's not locked down? USB ports. The attackers gained access to your network using their customized hardware security key to bypass kiosk mode.

data.name: Compromised Virtual Host
data.description: The management port for a virtual host was not segmented from the corporate network and the attackers used the default credentials to gain access to all guest hosts running on the hypervisor.

data.name: Corrupted Employee
data.description: The attackers are part of a ransomware gang that solicited employees of your company to willfully give over their credentials in exchange for a portion of the ransom paid. Bobby took the bait.

data.name: Malicious Extension
data.description: An Entra ID Global Admin unknowingly installed a malicious browser extension created by the attackers then authenticated to the Entra ID portal. The attackers hijacked the session token, impersonated the admin, and compromised Entra ID.

data.name: Golden Ticket Attack
data.description: The attackers, W1llyW0nka and his 00mpa L00mpas, discover a backup of the ntds.dit and system hive files in a directory that is accessible by everyone. The attackers use these files to generate forged Kerberos tickets that allow them to impersonate any user in your domain.

data.name: Misconfigured Certificate Templates (ESC1)
data.description: Years ago, a client authentication certificate template was created for a development environment. Not soon after, that template was forgotten. But don't worry; the friendly attackers just found it for you and are currently impersonating your Domain Admin.

data.name: Overprivileged Group Policy/High Profile GPO
data.description: The attackers find a Group Policy Object (GPO) linked to the domain root which allows "Authenticated Users" to modify it. They use Restricted Groups to elevate to the domain's Administrator.

data.name: Passwords in AD Attribute
data.description: The attackers dump all user attributes from Active Directory and discover an admin user's password in a non-standard attribute field which allows them to log in as Domain Admin.

data.name: Overprivileged Cloud Application
data.description: The attackers discover that a standard user owns an application that has "Directory.ReadWrite.All" permissions to your company's Entra ID tenant and leverages them to gain full admin rights.

data.name: vCenter Console Coercion
data.description: The attackers gain access to vCenter and perform a Denial of Service (DOS) attack against Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) on a Domain Controller (DC). A Domain Admin logs in to troubleshoot using vCenter, allowing the attackers to share the session.

data.name: Server Management Compromise
data.description: The attackers scan the network and discover that a dedicated remote management channel is available and running outdated server firmware. They utilize a known vulnerability to give them control over your server.

data.name: GIFs as C2
data.description: The attackers use malicious GIFs within the enterprise messaging application to relay reverse shell communications. Laugh now, cry later. :D

data.name: Living Off Trusted Sites (LOTS)
data.description: The attackers exfiltrate data from your network using a site in your trusted sites list that is also on the Living Off Trusted Sites (LOTS) Project.

data.name: AdminSDHolder Rights Modification
data.description: The AdminSDHolder process is designed to protect sensitive groups. The attackers grant themselves access to modify the AdminSDHolder object, allowing them to regain access even when permissions are removed.

data.name: Cloud Application Impersonation
data.description: The attackers find a cloud application that is using a password key with access to a Managed Identity in your Entra ID instance. The admin stored the key in the application's description field, which allows the attackers to maintain a foothold in your environment.

data.name: Bear vs. Powerstation
data.description: A bear attacked the power substation for your datacenter. Don't worry, he's down, but so is your datacenter. The only thing worse than the smell is not having a hot backup facility.
data.notes: The defenders lose 1 turn as they discuss the difference between a hot backup and a cold backup.

data.name: Ghosted by AV
data.description: A recent unverified update caused all endpoints to alarm on false positives. A useless antivirus is as good as no AV at all. Do you shut it down or keep it running while sifting through all the noise?
data.notes: The Defenders receive a -3 modifier on Endpoint Security Protection Analysis for the rest of the session.

data.name: DiscountConsultant.lol
data.description: Ever since hiring Scott, this incident response has gone from bad to worse. He had us chasing the wrong lead the whole time. Turns out, our consultant has no real IR experience despite a senior title. Luckily, he has red team experience and recognizes the TTPs.
data.notes: The Defenders must roll a die. If the die is even, the Incident Captain must reveal the Initial Compromise card. If the die is odd, the Incident Captain must draw another Persistence card.

data.name: Trimarc123!
data.description: The attackers' access to your network just fell into their laps. The local admin account on all workstations share the same password, so if the attackers gained admin on one workstation, they can now log in to them all.
data.notes: If one of the Defenders can accurately explain LAPS, the Incident Captain must reveal the Pivot & Escalate card. Otherwise, the Incident Captain must draw an additional Pivot & Escalate card.

data.name: Dude, Where's Our Docs?
data.description: The project to fully document important incident response procedures was not started on time and never finished.
data.notes: The Defenders no longer have a +3 modifier on their Established Procedure cards.

data.name: Click, Click, Boom
data.description: Instead of buying new hard drives, you decided to save some money on "refurbished" drives. Don't worry, you didn't use those drives on anything important -- only your SIEM -- ya know, that system you spend all that money on and don't use.
data.notes: SIEM Log Analysis is unavailable to the Defenders for the rest of the session.

data.name: Peekaboo
data.description: Remember that DIY security camera you set up to keep an eye on your servers? Well, you forgot to secure it and change the default password, so now the bad guys know all of your secrets.
data.notes: The Incident Captain must draw an additional Initial Compromise card.

data.name: Product Trials and Tribulation
data.description: Your marketing team is demoing a new piece of software without letting the security group know. Your EDR lights up like a Christmas tree with unusual activity, slowing its analysis to a crawl.
data.notes: Endpoint Security Protection Analysis is unavailable for the next 3 turns.

data.name: Jake Hildreth
data.description: The Defenders get an extra (3) turns to complete the session
data.quote: "We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit." — Will Durant

data.name: Dev Badlu
data.description: The Defenders must reveal the C2 and Exfil card
specialties: Building Tools to Help Combat Human Trafficking
data.quote: "Security is like an onion, the more layers you have the more crying the red team is going to be doing." — Dev

data.name: Sean Metcalf
data.description: The Defenders choose any one of the scenario cards to be revealed
data.quote: "The question every organization has to answer for themselves is do they want to take the red pill & learn their security issues or the blue pill and continue thinking everything is fine." — Sean

data.name: Brandon Colley
data.description: The Defenders get to choose an additional (2) Consultant Cards
data.quote: "Make a decision, even if it’s wrong." — Dad

data.name: SEANbot
data.description: The Defenders choose between one and three turns and receive a +3 modifier but also lose that number of turns

data.name: Application Runtime Analysis
data.description: The Defenders use their Application Runtime Security solution to view process tree traces of attacks against their applications.

data.name: Cloud Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis
data.description: The Defenders use Cloud SIEM to aggregate logs from the cloud provider, applications, and devices to identify abnormal patterns, such as unusual access, traffic, or attack signatures.

data.name: Cloud Identity and Entitlement Management (CIEM)
data.description: The Defenders use CIEM (pronounced kim) to determine the potential overprivileged paths to sensitive access. They learn the names of the roles and the Identity and Access Management (IAM) users that are risky.

data.name: Workload Protection
data.description: The Defenders use their cloud-native workload protection software to understand commands that were executed on the compromised workload.

data.name: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) Analysis
data.description: The Defenders use an inventory of SBOM to correlate whether or not a specific software package is present in their environment.

data.name: Compromised Single Sign-On (SSO) Federated Identity
data.description: The attackers compromised an SSO federated identity and leveraged that identity to authenticate to your organization's cloud environments.

data.name: Poisoned Cloud Image Supply Chain
data.description: The attackers created a malicious cloud image with a doppelgänger name for the legitimate image and your Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tools used it instead of the intended artifact, resulting in their full control of your virtual machine.

data.name: Cloud-Native Serverless Function Compromised
data.description: The attackers compromised a serverless function via an injection. They gained access to the credentials for the functions role, any data it has access to, and network resources in the same Virtual Private Cloud (VPC).

data.name: Confused Deputy Attack
data.description: The attackers abused a misconfiguration found in a role created by the cloud service provider allowing them to assume roles to gain access and read/write data.

data.name: Github Action Compromised
data.description: The attackers backdoored your self-hosted GitHub Action runner, compromising the runtime of your CI/CD job giving them access to read code, environment variables, and secrets that are sensitive.

data.name: Backdoored Software Supply Chain
data.description: The attackers modified an open-source library that downloads malicious code on a developer's machine.

data.name: Cloud Application Compromised
data.description: A web application running an enterprise-class framework has a maximum level Common Vulnerability Exposure (CVE) that allows an attacker to execute arbitrary code.

data.name: Exposed Cloud Credentials via Unauthenticated Kubernetes Dashboard
data.description: The attackers discovered an exposed Kubernetes Dashboard allowing unauthenticated access to the API, allowing them to launch workloads and access data.

data.name: Credentials Exposed in Storage Bucket
data.description: The attackers enumerate buckets and identify long-lived credentials in files that allow authentication as a cloud administrator.

data.name: Instance Takeover via User Data
data.description: The attackers identify an overly privileged compute workload and modify user data to gain shell access, allowing them to leverage the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) to retrieve an administrative credential.

data.name: Kubernetes Service Account PrivEsc
data.description: The attackers compromise a high-privileged service account mounted in a Kubernetes pod.

data.name: Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) Access
data.description: The attackers exploit Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) on a cloud-hosted web app to gain access to the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS). This allows them to gain temporary security credentials they use to pivot in your cloud environment.

data.name: Credential Store Compromise
data.description: The attackers gain access to a cloud-hosted credential store containing various user and application credentials via a permissions misconfiguration.

data.name: Identity and Access Management (IAM) Policy Abuse
data.description: The attackers discover that policies enforced for certain roles and resources allow them to escalate privileges within the cloud account.

data.name: Backdoored Container Image
data.description: The attackers modify a container image to include malicious code that gets executed every time it is started.

data.name: Additional Credential Creation
data.description: The attackers create a second set of credentials for a user.

data.name: Cloned Kubernetes Credentials
data.description: The attackers clone privileged system accounts with long-lasting credentials.

data.name: Backdoored Role Trust Policy
data.description: The attackers update the trust policy for an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, allowing them to assume the role from an account you do not control.

data.name: Living Off the Cloud as Exfil
data.description: The attackers use cloud provider Command Line Interface (CLI) tools to exfiltrate data.

data.name: Snapshotting Resources as Exfil
data.description: The attackers take a snapshot of a virtual machine or database and replicate to an account you do not control.

data.name: Software as a Service (SaaS) Tunneling Virtual Private Network (VPN) as C2
data.description: The attackers deploy a commercial tunneling VPN client to the compromised asset.

data.name: Undocumented Application Programming Interfaces (API)
data.description: The attackers have performed their actions using undocumented cloud provider APIs, and none of their activity is showing up in your SIEM solution. Your Cloud SIEM can no longer trust the data coming from your cloud provider. The Cloud Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis Detection is unavailable for the next 3 turns.

data.name: Attacker Stops Cloud Logging
data.description: The attackers stop control plane logging altogether, making the security team blind to future attacker behavior. Choose one Defender to skip 2 turns while they deal with the high-severity incident.

data.name: Cloud Security Training
data.description: Your security engineers downloaded Stratus Red Team and have simulated dozens of attacks in a controlled setting. They identified gaps in their current Detections and made improvements. The Defenders get a +3 modifier for the Cloud Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis card for the remainder of the session.

data.name: Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2) Project Complete
data.description: Your security engineers completed a year-long project that removed all use of IMDSv1 in your environment, eliminating the chance that a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) can be used to gain access to cloud credentials. The Incident Captain must reveal the Pivot and Escalate card while eating a celebratory slice of New York pizza.

data.name: Supply Chain Firewall
data.description: Your team has introduced the supply chain firewall into all developer and continuous integration (CI) workstreams reducing the likelihood that one of your developers can be compromised by a supply chain attack. The Incident Captain must reveal the Persistence card.

data.name: Public Storage Bucket Exposed
data.description: A cloud storage service was misconfigured to allow public access. The bucket contained Personally Identifiable Information (PII) for thousands of your customers. The Defenders must play their Crisis Management Detection. If they are successful, they can move past this issue. If they aren't, they receive a -2 modifier on all detections for the rest of the session.

data.name: Exposed Sofware as a Service (SaaS) Application Programming Interface (API) Key During Public Presentation
data.description: One of your engineers just gave an amazing presentation, sharing an epic story about how your company uses a SaaS product. Unfortunately, they forgot to redact their SaaS API key. Members of the audience quickly logged in and accessed your company resources. Accidents happen, but what do you do when someone exposes your organization inadvertently? The Incident Captain must draw an additional Pivot and Escalate card.

data.name: Third-Party Code Library Compromised
data.description: Your developer proactively ran GuardDog Command Line Interface (CLI) scans on a Python package before using it, and flagged the package as malicious, thereby avoiding a compromise. This encouraged more developers in your organization to also use GuardDog before integrating new packages into their software. The Defenders get a +3 modifier for the Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) card for the remainder of the session.

data.name: Missing HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) Protection
data.description: By having HTTP to HTTPS redirects, the attackers can "strip" SSL from a session. The attackers need to be on the same network for this to work. So, think coffee shops... evil, coffee shops.

data.name: Supply Chain Attack
data.description: The attackers insert malware in the update process of one of your key enterprise management tools. This gives them direct access to the heart of your infrastructure.

data.name: Physical Access
data.description: The attackers gain physical access to your organization and use this to pivot to your internal networks.

data.name: SMB Weakness
data.description: The attackers take advantage of a number of different Server Message Block (SMB) issues that can be used for post-exploitation. From SMB Signing disabled to using SMBv1.

data.name: Internal Spearphishing
data.description: The attackers leverage existing access to users' email to send attack emails to other targets. Because they come from the inside, the attack emails tend to bypass security controls.

data.name: Access Token Manipulation
data.description: The attackers conduct actions under other user/service account tokens.

data.name: Stale Network Address Configurations (SNAC) Attack
data.description: The attackers take advantage of a system or a network service that has been configured with a hard-coded IP address or fully qualified domain name (FQDN) that is no longer associated with a live host.

data.name: Cleartext Passwords in Files
data.description: The attackers love people who share and save passwords in files everyone else can read. This attack works because people (often admins and developers) create documents and spreadsheets with passwords in them. Then, they put them on shares that are readable to everyone in the domain.

data.name: Event Triggered Malware
data.description: The attackers' malware triggers only when specific events occur. For example, when a specific DLL or service is started.

data.name: Malware Injection Into Client Software
data.description: The attackers insert their malware to run alongside (or in) third-party software. Stuxnet and Bonadan did this.

data.name: Malicious Email Rules
data.description: The attackers create rules in an email inbox and/or client that trigger on specific events or when certain keywords are present in a message.

data.name: Windows Service Recovery Actions
data.description: The attackers use Windows Service failure recovery actions as a means of persistence on an accessible service they can remotely crash on demand.

data.name: Registry Keys for Persistence
data.description: The attackers add/modify registry commands to cause their malware to run on system startup and/or user login. This has been around forever. Almost every piece of solid malware in existence can do this.

data.name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium
data.description: The attackers use a USB drive, printouts, or even socks... yes, socks, as a way to get data out of a network. This requires an accomplice on the inside or it can be used with the Insider Threat (Initial Compromise) card.
tools: USB drive/socks and a dream… a dream of evil.

data.name: Call a Consultant
data.description: Do you want help? Feeling stuck? Rolling badly? Need a different perspective on the incident? Then maybe it's time to phone a friend. You can choose one Consultant Card to help your team with the incident. The Consultant Card's modifier is effective immediately.

data.name: Physical Security Review
data.description: Do you have security cameras? Do you have security guards? Do you have access badges for certain areas in your facilities? Can just anyone access your sensitive IT infrastructure? No? Are you sure?

data.name: Food Poisoning
data.description: The life of this organization depends upon just one thing: finding someone back there who can not only work this incident, but who didn't have fish for dinner.
data.notes: Each of the Defenders must roll a D20 and the person with the lowest number will finish the session by themselves without any assistance from the others.

data.name: SIEM Goes Down
data.description: No SIEM for you!
data.notes: It is discovered that due to an intern error, your logging server/SIEM has not been logging properly for the last two weeks. All SIEM actions are off the table for the rest of the session.

data.name: This Isn't the First Time, and Won't Be the Last
data.description: This is not the first time the attackers have been on your network.
data.notes: Through forensic analysis, it has been discovered that the backdoor had internal DNS servers’ IP addresses hard-coded in them because the attackers have been in before. Have the Incident Captain draw an additional Persistence Card.

data.name: EDR Compromise
data.description: The attackers gain access to your Endpoint Protection suite of tools.
data.notes: Endpoints stop reporting to the EDR console… The attackers found a console session that hadn’t timed out yet and issued mass uninstalls. All Endpoint Security Protection Analysis actions are unavailable for the rest of the session.

data.name: Attackers Taunt You
data.description: The attackers call out the security team, via a message to every system on the network.
data.notes: The attackers use msg command to send a pop-up to incident responders, "Shall we play a game?"

data.name: Attackers Timestomp Key Evidence Files
data.description: (-3) Modifier for Log-Related Actions There are tools that allow attackers to modify Modified-Accessed-Created-Entry (MACE) timestamps of files. One such tool is in Metasploit called Timestomp.
data.notes: The attackers can change the MACE for their malware to be in the future. What does this do to your handling of evidence? Can you trust timestamps at all?

data.name: No Good Deed Goes Unpunished...
data.description: The Purple Team uncovers another incident.
data.notes: When tuning your detection capabilities during a purple team engagement (unrelated to the incident at hand), your team detects another attack. You now have two compromises to deal with. Have the Incident Captain pull another set of Attack Cards. The Defenders get five extra turns.

data.name: Our Friend, Hacky
data.description: You discover other attackers have been on your network for months.
data.notes: Have the Incident Captain draw an additional Initial Compromise Card.

data.name: Is it Getting Hot in Here?
data.description: HVAC systems are important... and they will fail at the worst times. This... is one of those times.
data.notes: Your data center HVAC system is infected with a worm. It’s supposed to be air-gapped. It is 103°F outside, and the server temperatures are rising. All servers need to be shut down. RIGHT NOW! Hope you have a "hot site."

data.name: Don't Forget to Smash the Subscribe Button!
data.description: Some attackers just want to watch the world burn.
data.notes: The attackers post a YouTube video detailing the extent of their attack because it wasn't getting the press they thought it deserved.
